source.title: Edo demonstratives and place words: this, that, these, those, here, there
source.note: Transcribed from a lesson slide photographed by the project owner. The slide has two tables (singular/plural demonstratives, and the two place words) and four worked example sentences.
source.language: Edo (Bini), Niger-Congo; main language of the ancient Kingdom of Benin
source.supplied_file: A file was also supplied at Downloads/'Edo words(there,here,this,these'. Despite having no extension it is an audio-only recording, 5m09s long — not the slide and not a video. No speech-to-text was available, so it has not been transcribed. If it teaches more of this lesson, that material is NOT represented here.
transcription_caveats: No tone marks were supplied. The slide marks only the underdot vowels (ọ, ẹ), ṅ in evbaṅ/evbaṅna, and ỹ in ỹọ. Add tone before teaching pronunciation.

The slide writes elisions with an apostrophe: vb' ọna for vbe ọna, ọr' for ọre, n' for ne, ỹ' for ỹọ. Entries below keep the slide's spelling and give the full form only where the slide itself supplies it.
vbe is glossed 'what' by position in example 1 only; edo-questions-grammar.md records de as 'what/which'. Whether these are the same morpheme is not settled here, so vbe is not added as a headword.
ọr' is read as ọre 'is / it is' from the slide's own gloss 'That is the thing'. The full form is not printed on the slide.

The ọ of ọni is silent once the word follows its noun — confirmed by the project owner, who supplied the slide. Recorded as elision of one word (see demonstratives.vowel_elision), not as a separate short form. Whether the plurals ena/eni behave the same way is still unconfirmed.

vowel_elision.rule: The project owner confirms the ọ of ọni is silent in a sentence. It is not a separate word: once the demonstrative follows the noun it modifies, the initial vowel drops and only ni is said and written — okhuo ni 'that woman' (example 4). Example 3 shows the same for ọna — ẹkpo na 'this bag'.
vowel_elision.vowel_kept_when: The full vowel is kept where the word stands alone or opens the sentence. Example 2 begins Ọni ọr' Emwin ... with the ọ intact, and example 1 has Vb' ọna khin?
vowel_elision.open_question: Whether the plurals ena and eni elide the same way is not shown on the slide and has not been confirmed.

examples.shows: ọna standing alone as the subject

examples.edo: Ọni ọr' Emwin n' u dẹh ra?
examples.literal: That is the thing that u bought or?
examples.shows: ọni opening the sentence, so the ọ is kept and pronounced; ra closes the question

examples.edo: Lahọ, mu Ẹkpo na ỹ' Evbani.
examples.literal: Please carry this bag put there
examples.shows: ọna with its ọ silent after the noun — ẹkpo na 'this bag'; evbani 'there'; the serial verb mu ... ỹọ 'carry ... put' = 'place'
ọni with its ọ silent after the noun — okhuo ni 'that woman'; evbaṅna 'here'

academy_vocabulary.example: Vb' ọna khin? — What is this?
Ọni ọr' Emwin n' u dẹh ra? — Is that what you bought?

academy_vocabulary.example: ẹkpo na — this bag (full form ọna)
